site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Rama Blesses the Bhil Hunter
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana · Aranya Kanda, Sarga 69 (Gita Press translation)
body: In the deep forest of Dandaka, the bhil hunter Guha welcomed Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana into his humble leaf-thatched hut. He watched over them through the night and offered the forest's bounty with quiet, unassuming care.
Rama was deeply moved by Guha's devotion and refused to let him accept gratitude in return. He embraced the hunter warmly, honoring the sincerity of his heart above the modesty of his dwelling.

Blessing Guha, Rama foretold that his descendants would one day be counted among the guardians of Ayodhya. The little cottage glowed with the light of that promise, a humble home made holy by love received.

stories.title: Prithu Chases the Wandering Cow
body: When King Prithu, son of Vena, saw his people starving, he learned that the Earth herself had taken the form of a cow and fled into the forests and hills, angered by long misrule. With quiet resolve, the king set out on foot to follow her hidden trail through the wild places.

Humble and reverent, Prithu addressed her as mother, bowing low among the trees and promising that his kingdom would protect and honor her from then on. His gentle words softened her anger, and she at last stopped running, resuming her own gracious form at his side.

In gratitude she yielded grain, fruit, and herbs in abundance across the fields, and Prithu established the first fair harvest. The people rejoiced with songs, and the land again offered its plenty under the king's just and caring rule.

stories.title: Shade of the Sacred Trees
body: On a warm afternoon in Vraja, young Krishna settled beneath the trees along the Yamuna, the branches cooling Him and His cowherd companions. The leaves rustled kindly overhead, offering their shelter to the playful band of boys and grazing cows.

Turning to Balarama, Krishna smiled and praised the giving nature of the trees, whose leaves, flowers, fruits, shade, bark, roots, and sap all exist for the welfare of others. He declared that a life spent offering shelter to every being is the true perfection of birth.

The boys listened with bright eyes and softly agreed, their hearts warmed by the gentle teaching. Peace returned to the pasture as the cowherds lingered by the riverbank, grateful for the trees' gift and the lesson that generosity itself is its own beautiful reward.

stories.title: The King Whose Calm Won Freedom
stories.source: The Jataka · Vol. III, Ekaraja Jataka (No. 303) — E. B. Cowell ed., public domain
body: A king was seized by a rival monarch and dragged into captivity, where cruelties were heaped upon him one after another. Yet he neither wept for mercy nor burned with rage; he met each blow with a stillness that startled his guards and softened the whispers in the court.

His captor, a fierce ruler grown used to fear, watched the prisoner bow his head without hatred and felt something in his own chest begin to thaw. Day after day the stranger's patience worked like warm oil on cold iron, until the captor could no longer bear the sight of his injustice.

At last the rival king unbound him, offered rich gifts, and asked forgiveness with downcast eyes. The two kings departed as friends, and word spread through the kingdoms that a steady heart, even in chains, can melt the fiercest soul.

stories.title: Mother Shandili's Gentle Welcome
stories.source: Panchatantra · Book 2, 'The Winning of Friends', Mother Shandili's Bargain — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: When a young brahmin newly wed arrived from a foreign country, courtiers at the royal palace laughed at his unknowing ways. But a kind old woman named Shandili saw his loneliness and quietly took him under her wing, teaching him the customs of the city as one would teach a younger sibling.

Patiently she guided him through every strange rule and unspoken rite, and before long the young brahmin won an honoured post at the royal court. Through her gentle teaching, the laughter faded and respect took its place.

Years later he built Shandili a fine house of her own, remembering that one steady guide is worth a thousand gold pieces. The young brahmin's gratitude is a tender reminder that compassion, offered without fanfare, shapes lives across many seasons.
